display_title: U.S. Suspends Tech Giants From Green Card Program

short_summary: The Trump administration has suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and major IT firms from a key permanent labor certification program over foreign hiring investigations.

sources.title: U.S. suspends Microsoft, Adobe from green card labor program in foreign worker crackdown

sources.title: Trump Administration Cuts Off Access to a Major Immigration Program for Workers at Microsoft and Adobe

paragraphs: The United States Department of Labor has officially announced the suspension of several major technology corporations, including Microsoft and Adobe, from a vital labor program amid an ongoing crackdown on foreign hiring. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling stated that the administration will no longer accept or process any new applications under the Permanent Labor Certification program, commonly known as PERM, for a host of prominent companies. In addition to Microsoft and Adobe, the targeted entities include Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro, and HCL, with Sonderling citing multiple active federal investigations into potential fraud and allegations that these organizations have undermined domestic job opportunities.

During a press conference on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance directed sharp criticism specifically at Microsoft. Vance claimed that the firm had laid off 6,000 workers in 2025 and replaced them with individuals on H-1B visas, which are designed for highly skilled positions that employers allegedly struggle to fill with qualified U.S. workers. While noting that the administration intends to maintain a great relationship with Microsoft, Vance stressed that they will deny the company the ability to apply for permanent residencies until it proves a commitment to putting American workers first. The Vice President also compared elements of the current immigration system to bringing indentured servants into the United States.

In response, Microsoft firmly defended its corporate recruitment strategies through an official statement. The technology giant emphasized that the vast majority of its domestic employees are American citizens. Furthermore, representatives clarified that of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications submitted in the last fiscal year, eighty percent were strictly to extend or change the legal status of existing Microsoft workers rather than onboard brand-new arrivals. The company noted that filings for new employees represented only one percent of its U.S. workforce, that it adheres to rigorous standards, and that its compensation for visa holders ranks among the highest across all filings.

Tech companies have relied heavily on foreign labor programs for decades. According to 2026 data, Amazon led all petitioners, followed closely by other major technology and consulting firms. Meanwhile, the administration's sweeping policy announcement coincided with a high-profile presidential event at the White House where Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, along with other prominent immigrant tech leaders such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and AMD CEO Su, were honored. Furthermore, the administration announced investigations into nine prestigious universities regarding the J-1 visa program, signaling a broader escalation of federal scrutiny over international employment and education pathways in Silicon Valley.

facts.fact: The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft, Adobe, and several IT companies from its Permanent Labor Certification program.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling stated the suspension is due to active federal investigations into potential fraud and undercutting American workers.
Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft heavily during a press conference regarding foreign hiring practices.
Microsoft defended its record, stating that 80 percent of its recent H-1B visa applications were to extend or change status for existing employees.
